items.question: Examine the salient features of the town planning and material culture of the Indus Valley Civilization, and discuss what they reveal about Harappan society.
items.modelAnswer: The Harappan cities display a remarkably standardised urban template. A **grid layout** with roads intersecting at right angles, a fortified **citadel** raised above a **lower town**, uniform **burnt-brick** construction, and a networked **covered drainage** system point to centralised civic planning and a strong civic authority. Public works such as the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro, granaries, and the tidal **dockyard at Lothal** indicate organised labour, surplus management and long-distance trade (with Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf). Craft specialisation — steatite **seals** with an undeciphered pictographic script, **cire perdue** bronzes like the Dancing Girl, and wheel-made red-and-black **pottery** — reflects a prosperous, occupationally differentiated society whose material uniformity across a vast area suggests shared cultural and administrative norms.
keyPoints: Grid-pattern streets meeting at right angles; citadel vs. lower town
Standardised burnt-brick construction and networked covered drainage
Public architecture: Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro), granaries, Lothal dockyard
Craft & trade: steatite seals, cire perdue bronzes, red-and-black pottery
Material uniformity over ~1.3 million sq km implies shared civic norms
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Art & Architecture)

items.question: Discuss the economy and trade of the Indus Valley Civilization, highlighting its agriculture, crafts and long-distance exchange.
items.modelAnswer: The Harappan economy rested on a productive **agricultural** base — **wheat and barley** were the staple crops, with fruits such as pomegranates and bananas; Kalibangan shows **plough marks** and double cropping, while Lothal gives early evidence of **rice**. A surplus supported specialised **crafts**: bead-making (stone, shell, ivory, faience), metalwork, and cotton and wool weaving. Trade was both internal and **long-distance**: Harappan seals and objects reach **Iraq (Mesopotamia)**, exchange was carried on with the **Persian Gulf and the Sumerians**, and **lapis lazuli** was obtained from **Afghanistan**. The accurate, standardised **weights and measures** found at the Lothal dock, and the dockyard itself, point to a regulated commercial system — the material foundation of Harappan urban prosperity.
keyPoints: Staple crops wheat and barley; plough marks at Kalibangan; rice at Lothal
Craft specialisation: beads, metalwork, cotton and wool weaving
Trade with the Persian Gulf and Sumerians; seals found in Iraq
Lapis lazuli sourced from Afghanistan
Accurate standardised weights and measures at the Lothal dock

items.question: Bring out the salient features of Harappan art and religion with suitable examples.
items.modelAnswer: Harappan **art** combined technical skill with realism. In bronze, the **cire perdue (lost-wax)** method produced the **Dancing Girl** in a tribhanga posture; in stone, the **Bearded Priest ('Priest-King')** wears a trefoil-patterned shawl with meditative half-closed eyes. **Terracotta** was used for toys and figurines, and wheel-made **Red-and-Black pottery** carried motifs of trees, birds, animals and geometric designs. **Religion** appears nature-linked: clay **Mother-Goddess** figures and the seated **Pashupati (proto-Shiva)** seal — a horned figure surrounded, in the APPSC source, by an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo — alongside sacred symbols such as the **Peepal tree** and the **Horned Bull**. Structures assigned ritual significance include the **Great Bath** and the **fire altars** at Kalibangan and Lothal, and three burial types (extended, symbolic, twin) reveal varied funerary belief. The absence of clearly identified temples and the prominence of seals point to a distinctive religious life.
keyPoints: Bronze Dancing Girl (cire perdue, tribhanga); stone Bearded Priest with trefoil shawl
Terracotta figurines/toys; wheel-made Red-and-Black painted pottery
Mother Goddess figures and the Pashupati (proto-Shiva) seal (identification not straightforward)
Sacred symbols: Peepal tree, Horned Bull; Great Bath and fire altars (Kalibangan, Lothal)
Three burial practices: extended, symbolic, twin

items.question: Critically examine the various theories proposed for the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization.
items.modelAnswer: The decline of the Harappan cities, placed around **1500 BCE** in the APPSC source (with the distinctive urban phase already ending by c. 1900 BCE per NCERT), has no single agreed cause; several theories are proposed. **Environmental** explanations dominate: a massive **flood** of the Indus and destructive eastward-moving **monsoons**; the **drying of the Saraswati River** from around **1900 BCE**, triggering prolonged **drought and famine**; and, by **1800 BCE**, a cooler, drier climate with a possible **tectonic event** diverting the rivers that were the civilization's lifelines. A **human** theory holds that nomadic Indo-European **Aryans** invaded, coinciding with the dated decline. Others suggest a **pandemic disease**. A **migration** hypothesis argues the Harappans shifted toward the **Ganges basin**, establishing villages and isolated farms. Since the evidence is fragmentary and no theory is conclusive, the fall is best understood as a **gradual, multi-causal** process rather than a single catastrophe.
keyPoints: Decline placed ~1500 BCE (APPSC source); urban phase ends by ~1900 BCE (NCERT); no conclusive single cause
Environmental: Indus floods, shifting monsoons, drought and famine
Drying of the Saraswati (from ~1900 BCE); tectonic river diversion by ~1800 BCE
Aryan invasion theory; pandemic disease theory
Migration toward the Ganges basin; best read as gradual and multi-causal

items.question: 'The Indus Valley Civilization was essentially an urban civilization of remarkable geographical extent.' Substantiate.
items.modelAnswer: The Harappan civilization was the **earliest known urban culture** of the north-western subcontinent and one of the world's first three, alongside Mesopotamia and Egypt. Its **urban character** is evident in planned, grid-patterned cities divided into citadel and lower town, standardised burnt-brick housing, covered drainage, granaries, public baths and the Lothal dockyard — all signs of civic organisation and surplus. Its **geographical extent** was exceptional: about **1.3 million sq km**, larger than the contemporary Egyptian or Mesopotamian cultures, stretching from **Sutkagendor** (west) to **Alamgirpur** (east) and from **Manda** (north) to **Daimabad** (south), across the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra basins. The striking **uniformity** of town planning, seals, weights and pottery across this vast area underlines a shared urban culture rather than a loose scatter of settlements.
keyPoints: Earliest known urban culture; one of the first three world civilizations
Urban markers: grid cities, citadel/lower town, drainage, granaries, dockyard
Extent ~1.3 million sq km — larger than Egypt or Mesopotamia
Boundary sites: Sutkagendor (W), Alamgirpur (E), Manda (N), Daimabad (S)
Uniform planning, seals, weights and pottery imply a shared urban culture
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: IVC (Introduction; Map & Sites; Art & Architecture)

items.question: 'The town planning of the Harappan cities reflects a sophisticated civic administration.' Discuss.
items.modelAnswer: Harappan urbanism implies coordinated public authority. Cities followed a **grid layout** with a raised **citadel (west)** over a **lower town (east)**, and used **baked bricks in a uniform 4:2:1 ratio** consistent across sites — a standardisation that no single household could enforce. **Covered street drains**, laid in some cities **before the houses**, with **cesspits at regular intervals**, point to sanitation planned and maintained **collectively**. Monumental public works — the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro, **granaries**, and the **tidal dockyard at Lothal** — required organised labour and surplus management, while **accurate chert weights** (binary then decimal, in multiples of 16) and standard **seals** imply regulated exchange. Scholars debate whether this reflects a **single centralised state**, several coordinated **city authorities**, or a well-ordered but ruler-less community; the absence of palaces and royal tombs cautions against assuming a monarchy. Nonetheless, the region-wide **uniformity of bricks, weights and layout** is strong evidence of an effective civic administration governing the Harappan cities.
keyPoints: Grid layout; citadel (west) over lower town (east); uniform 4:2:1 bricks across sites
Covered street drainage with cesspits, sometimes laid before houses — collective sanitation
Public works: Great Bath, granaries, Lothal dockyard — organised labour and surplus
Standardised chert weights (binary then decimal) and seals imply regulated exchange
Debate: single state vs many city authorities vs ruler-less order; uniformity implies effective civic administration

items.question: Was the Harappan civilization a single state or a society without rulers? Examine the debate on Harappan authority, including the 'priest-king' hypothesis.
items.modelAnswer: The nature of Harappan authority is inferred from material evidence rather than texts, and remains debated. Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, **no temples or palaces** have been conclusively identified; a large Mohenjo-daro building once called a 'palace' yielded **no rich finds**, and there are **no royal tombs** or monarchic iconography. The steatite bust conventionally named the **'Priest-King'** rests on an **analogy with Mesopotamia** and is **not proven** — there is no evidence of a priestly ruler. Against this, the **extraordinary uniformity** of pottery, seals, chert weights and the **4:2:1 brick ratio** across a vast area argues for a **standardising authority** capable of enforcing norms. Scholars therefore propose three models: a **single centralised state**; **several rulers or city-states** sharing a culture; or a **relatively egalitarian** society coordinated **without a single ruler**. On balance, the evidence supports organised, standardising authority but **not a personalised kingship** on the Egyptian or Mesopotamian model — best described as coordination without a demonstrable king.
keyPoints: No temples or palaces conclusively identified; Mohenjo-daro 'palace' was find-poor; no royal tombs
The 'Priest-King' label is a Mesopotamian analogy — unproven
Region-wide uniformity (seals, chert weights, 4:2:1 bricks) implies a standardising authority
Three models: single state / several rulers / egalitarian no-ruler society
Conclusion: organised standardising authority, but not a personalised kingship like Egypt or Mesopotamia

items.question: Examine the survival and continuity of Harappan culture in the present times.
items.modelAnswer: This is a genuine APPSC Group-1 Mains 2023 (Paper-II, SAE-105) question, and it asks how Harappan cultural elements persist. Several **material and craft continuities** are argued: **cotton** — attested at Harappan sites — remained a defining Indian textile fibre; **bead-making** (notably **carnelian**, whose red colour the Harappans obtained by firing) survives in traditions such as the agate/carnelian work of Gujarat; and **shell-working** (as at Nageshwar and Balakot) continued as bangle and ornament craft. In **agriculture**, staples like **wheat and barley** and ox-drawn **ploughing** (implied by the bull on seals and terracotta plough models from Cholistan and Banawali) carried forward. In **weights, measures and craft standardisation**, the Harappan concern with regulated exchange prefigures later systems. **Religious and symbolic continuities** are often highlighted — the seated horned figure read (cautiously) as **'proto-Shiva'/Pashupati**, the veneration of the **Peepal tree** and the **bull**, and **Mother-Goddess** worship — though such identifications are interpretive and must be advanced with care. The balanced view is that while the Harappan urban system itself ended, a number of its **crafts, agricultural practices and cultural motifs plausibly persisted** into later Indian traditions, even if direct one-to-one links are debated.
keyPoints: Genuine APPSC Group-1 Mains 2023, Paper-II (SAE-105), Section I question
Craft continuities: cotton textiles, carnelian bead-making, shell-working (bangles)
Agricultural continuities: wheat/barley, ox-drawn ploughing
Symbolic/religious continuities (interpretive): proto-Shiva/Pashupati, peepal and bull veneration, Mother-Goddess worship
Balanced conclusion: crafts/practices/motifs plausibly persisted, though direct links are debated
